Resting-state functional connectivity is a neuroimaging technique that measures how different brain regions communicate with each other when a person is not performing a specific task. By observing these spontaneous fluctuations, we can map the brain's default communication networks. In this study, we focused on the thalamus and three key cortical regions: the medial prefrontal cortex (involved in self-reflection and decision-making), the posterior cingulate cortex (a hub for memory and self-referential thought), and the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (crucial for working memory and executive control).

Alterations in sensorimotor processing are highly common in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) $^{1-4}$ .
To appreciate why this matters, consider that sensorimotor processing is the foundation upon which all higher-level cognition is built.
Many studies have found evidence for altered auditory processing $^{5,6}$ , tactile processing $^{7,8}$ , visual processing $^{9}$ , and motor learning $^{10}$ in various age groups in ASD.

For instance, an individual with ASD might experience a loud noise as physically painful (auditory) or find the texture of clothing overwhelming (tactile). These are not merely annoyances; they are fundamental shifts in how the brain encodes reality.
Such sensorimotor differences have been linked to core symptoms of repetitive behaviors and socio-communicative deficits $^{8,11-15}$ .

Why would a difference in how we feel touch lead to social difficulties? The connection lies in the fact that social interaction is inherently sensorimotor. Reading a face, interpreting tone of voice, and coordinating body language all require rapid, accurate processing of sensory inputs. If the "switchboard" (thalamus) is sending noisy or distorted signals to the cortex, the brain may struggle to integrate these social cues effectively, leading to the communicative challenges characteristic of ASD.

processing is hypothesized to play a pivotal role in disrupted cognitive functions attributed to ASD, such as information processing, central coherence, perceptual integration, language development, and reading emotions from faces $^{1,16,17}$ .

Central coherence, for example, refers to the ability to see the "big picture" rather than getting lost in details. If sensory integration is impaired, the brain may default to processing local details (like the texture of a shirt) rather than the global context (the social situation), a phenomenon often observed in ASD.

This relationship between sensorimotor processing and core symptoms of ASD has been well-studied in younger cohorts. In older cohorts, however, past studies have combined adults with other age groups with limited behavioral and self-report data $^{18-20}$ .
This methodological mixing can obscure the unique neurological profile of adults.

Even though adults with ASD overwhelmingly experience unusual sensory processing similarly to their younger counterparts $^{21}$ , the link between sensorimotor processing and its underlying neurophysiology in adults is poorly explored, highlighting an important clinical need.
Understanding the adult brain is critical because it allows for the development of targeted interventions that respect the maturity and complexity of the adult experience.

To understand why sensorimotor processing is a focal point, we must first look at the chemical underpinnings of the brain.
Sensorimotor processing may be related to aberrant inhibitory neurotransmission in ASD.
Think of the brain as a complex electrical circuit board; for it to function correctly, it needs a balance between excitation (turning signals on) and inhibition (turning signals off).
Altered cortical inhibition is a widely supported theory in ASD, as evidenced by altered levels of glutamate $^{22}$
(the primary excitatory neurotransmitter, acting like the "gas pedal")
(the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, acting like the "brakes"),
If the brakes are faulty, the brain may become overwhelmed by sensory input, leading to the hypersensitivity often seen in autism. This isn't an isolated issue; neurodevelopmental

disorders associated with ASD, such as fragile X Syndrome and Tourette syndrome, also exhibit alterations of cortical inhibition and suggest an involvement of sensorimotor deficits $^{25,26}$ . Taken together, cortical excitability and sensorimotor processing appear to play an important role in the neurobiology of ASD.
In addition to cortical inhibition, the thalamus has been shown to be associated with the neurobiology of ASD.
To grasp the significance of this, imagine the thalamus as the brain's central "switchboard" or "air traffic control tower."

The thalamus is a critical functional hub for relaying sensory information to the cortex and modulating motor signals $^{27}$ . It does so by exerting fine-tuned inhibitory control over cortico-cortical and subcortical-cortical signaling $^{18,28}$ .

In other words, it doesn't just pass messages along; it filters them, ensuring that only relevant information reaches the higher processing centers of the brain. The clinical importance of this filtering role is highlighted by treatments

such as deep brain stimulation targeting the thalamus at the anterior nucleus and the ventral intermediate nucleus are known to reduce seizures in epilepsy $^{29}$ and reduce tremors in Parkinson's disease $^{30}$ , respectively.
By stimulating these specific thalamic nuclei, doctors can effectively "reset" the inhibitory balance, calming down overactive neural circuits.
This inhibitory role of the thalamus in motor processing and the evidence of cortical disinhibition shown in ASD suggest that the connectivity of the thalamus may differ in individuals with ASD.
If the switchboard is malfunctioning, the entire network suffers.

Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) has been a widely used tool in assessing co-fluctuations (or functional connectivity; FC) across brain regions in the absence of task-related cognitive demand $^{31,32}$ .

To understand this technique, consider that the brain is never truly "off." Even when you are lying still, doing nothing, different regions of your brain are talking to each other. rsfMRI captures these spontaneous conversations.

The task-free nature of rsfMRI has several key benefits, including higher participant compliance and the ability to aggregate data across multiple sites, that enable its widespread use in investigating thalamocortical FC in individuals with ASD.
This is particularly valuable for studying populations like adults with ASD, who may find complex cognitive tasks stressful or difficult to perform consistently.

An early neuroimaging study of children and adolescents with ASD using rsfMRI found evidence of thalamocortical hyperconnectivity in limbic, auditory, and motor regions, as well as general hypo-connectivity with regions involved in executive functioning and social cognition $^{33}$ .
In simpler terms, the "switchboard" was talking *too much* to the emotional, hearing, and movement centers, but *too little* to the centers responsible for planning and social understanding.

Another investigation that included children, adolescents, and adults from the autism brain imaging data exchange (ABIDE), a multisite neuroimaging database, also revealed widespread thalamic hyperconnectivity with temporal, sensorimotor, and prefrontal cortices with limited evidence of hypoconnectivity. However, these results were primarily driven by adolescents. Importantly, this study's investigation of the relationship between thalamocortical connectivity and ASD symptoms is inconclusive due to a lack of behavioral data $^{18}$ .
Without knowing the specific symptoms of the participants, it is hard to say if the brain patterns directly caused the behavioral traits.

Other studies that included adults did not use functionally distinct regions-of-interest (ROIs) $^{19}$ and did not examine the differences in thalamocortical connectivity between adults and adolescents $^{34}$ , obscuring the neurobiology of thalamocortical connectivity in adults alone. Thus, the results from these combined cohort studies are not representative of HFASD. In fact, no study to date has investigated thalamocortical connectivity specifically in HFASD and its relationship with ASD characteristics.

The overarching goal of this study was to examine thalamocortical FC in the less-studied ASD subpopulation of high functioning adults compared to an age- and sex-matched control group and analyze its relationship with clinical symptoms. We used a generalized linear model (GLM)-based approach for seed-based connectivity analysis and included seeds from the left and right thalami.

To break this down: a "seed" is a specific starting point in the brain from which we measure how strongly other areas are connected to it. By using the thalami as seeds, we could directly map the "switchboard's" connections to the rest of the brain.

We additionally used a cortical seed-based approach for analyzing thalamocortical FC $^{18}$ and included seeds from the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), and left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). These seeds allowed us to examine FC in the two most commonly studied resting state networks in ASD, default mode (DMN) $^{35-37}$ and central executive (CEN) $^{38-42}$ .
The DMN is active when you are daydreaming or reflecting on yourself, while the CEN is active when you are focused on a task.

These networks have shown altered connectivity with sensorimotor regions in previous studies of adolescents with ASD $^{37}$ and are known to engage the thalamus as a key functional region $^{27,43}$ . Then, we examined brain-behavior relationships by correlating observed group differences with clinical markers of ASD. Furthermore, we explored the effects of age and sex on these relationships using mediation and moderation analyses predicting ASD symptom severity. Lastly, we sought to validate our results in a separate, larger cohort of HFASD from the ABIDE public database $^{44,45}$ . By studying thalamocortical connectivity
in HFASD, we hope to better understand the neural correlates of differential sensorimotor processing in a specific and understudied population.

To ensure our findings are robust and not merely an artifact of a specific group of participants, we validated our results in a separate, independent cohort. We identified 58 individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and 51 typically developing (TD) individuals from the ABIDE database. Crucially, these participants were carefully matched to our primary HFASD cohort based on age, sex, and IQ (see Table 2). This matching process is essential because it controls for confounding variables, allowing us to isolate the effects of ASD itself rather than differences in demographics or cognitive ability. The detailed selection criteria are provided in the Supplemental Information. The functional brain imaging data from this new group were analyzed using the exact same methods described below, ensuring consistency across both datasets.

### fMRI preprocessing

Supplemental Table 2 outlines the specific MRI acquisition parameters used for both the HFASD and ABIDE cohorts. To handle the raw data, we preprocessed the functional data from both cohorts identically using **fMRIPrep v1.3.1** [52]. Think of fMRIPrep as an automated, high-quality assembly line for brain data. It integrates tools from various established neuroimaging software packages to standardize the cleaning and alignment of the data, which is critical for comparing results across different studies and cohorts.

A major challenge in fMRI analysis is **motion**. Even tiny head movements can create massive artifacts in the data, mimicking or obscuring true brain activity. To address this, we extracted several **nuisance regressors**—statistical variables that represent noise sources we want to remove from our signal. Specifically, we tracked:
*   **Framewise displacement (FD):** A metric that quantifies how much the head moved between consecutive time points (frames).
*   **Average cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) signal:** The signal intensity from the fluid surrounding the brain.
*   **Average white matter (WM) signal:** The signal intensity from the brain's white matter tracts.
*   **Global signal:** The average signal intensity across the entire brain.

By monitoring these, we can statistically "subtract" the noise associated with movement and physiological fluctuations.

Let’s look at the quality of the data in terms of motion. In the HFASD cohort, the group-mean FD was 0.162 for the ASD group and 0.143 for the TD group. A two-sample t-test revealed no significant difference between these groups ($p=0.4029$). Similarly, in the ABIDE cohort, the group-mean FD was 0.124 for ASD and 0.123 for TD, again showing no significant difference ($p=0.8679$). This is a crucial finding: it tells us that the ASD and TD participants moved their heads similarly during the scan. Therefore, any differences we find in brain activity later cannot be blamed on one group moving more than the other.

To further ensure data quality, we applied a technique called **motion scrubbing**. We censored (removed) any frames where the FD exceeded 0.5 mm. We also removed one frame before and two frames after any "offending" high-motion frame. Why? Because the brain's hemodynamic response (the blood flow change we measure) lags behind neural activity and takes several seconds to return to baseline. So, if a participant moves their head, the data immediately before and after that moment is likely corrupted. By removing these adjacent frames, we protect the integrity of the remaining time series.

After this scrubbing process, we checked how much data remained. In the HFASD cohort, the group-mean number of remaining frames (out of a total of 240) was 220.96 for ASD and 222.24 for TD ($p=0.8954$). In the ABIDE cohort, the group-mean percentage of frames remaining was 96.25% for ASD and 97.16% for TD ($p=0.2806$). Again, there is no significant difference between groups, confirming that the data quality is comparable.

We set a strict threshold for inclusion: any participant who retained less than 80% of their time points (TRs) after motion scrubbing was excluded from the analysis. This ensures that every participant in our final dataset has a robust amount of usable data. As a result, we analyzed 20 TD participants and 23 ASD participants from the HFASD cohort (Table 1). From the ABIDE cohort, we analyzed 51 TD participants and 58 ASD participants (Table 2). Further details of these preprocessing steps are described in the Supplemental Information.

### Seed-based correlation analysis

To understand how different parts of the brain communicate, we performed a **seed-based correlation analysis**. This method asks: "If I look at the activity in one specific brain region (the 'seed'), how does that activity fluctuate in sync with activity in other regions?"

We began by focusing on the **thalamus**, a critical relay station in the brain. We individually seeded the left and right thalami. To do this, we extracted the average time-series of all voxels (3D pixels) within the region defined by the **Harvard-Oxford thalamus probabilistic atlas**, thresholded at 90%. This atlas provides a standardized map of where the thalamus is located in the brain, and the 90% threshold ensures we are only including voxels that are very likely to be part of the thalamus, minimizing contamination from neighboring structures.

Next, we created seeds for three other key regions involved in higher-order cognitive and social processing: the **medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)**, the **posterior cingulate cortex (PCC)**, and the **left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC)**. For these regions, we used spherical regions of interest (ROIs) with a radius of 5 mm.

"Scrubbing" is a technique where time points with too much head movement are flagged and excluded from the analysis, or their influence is minimized, to prevent motion from distorting the connectivity results.
The first-level GLM analysis was run using FSL FEAT $^{55}$ .
FSL (FMRIB Software Library) is a standard toolkit for analyzing brain imaging data.
The resulting parameter estimates for each participant were incorporated in a higher-level GLM, which included any variables with significant group differences as covariates.

This is a two-step process: first, we analyze each person individually (first-level), and then we compare the groups (second-level). Including variables with significant group differences as covariates ensures that when we compare the groups, we are controlling for factors that already differ between them.

This higher-level GLM analysis was run using FSL randomise $^{56}$ , a permutation-based method that uses threshold-free cluster enhancement to correct for family-wise error rate in order to determine brain areas with group differences in parameter estimates between TD

(Autism Spectrum Disorder).

*   **Permutation-based method:** Instead of assuming the data follows a specific statistical distribution (like a bell curve), this method shuffles the group labels thousands of times to create a "null" distribution. This is more robust when the data doesn't fit standard assumptions.
*   **Threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE):** This is a sophisticated way to identify significant brain regions. It doesn't just look for the highest peaks; it also considers the size and shape of the clusters of activity. This helps find smaller, but still meaningful, areas of difference that might be missed by simpler methods.
*   **Family-wise error rate (FWER) correction:** Since we are testing millions of voxels, the chance of finding a "false positive" by random luck is high. FWER correction adjusts the significance threshold to account for this multiple testing problem.

We are testing five different seeds, so we divide our standard alpha level (0.05) by 5 to get 0.01. This stricter threshold ensures that we don't claim a finding is significant just because we looked in five different places.

The ABIDE (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange) is a large, independent dataset. Validating findings in a separate, larger group is a crucial step in scientific rigor; it proves that our results aren't just a fluke specific to our small sample.

Different hospitals (sites) use different MRI machines and settings. "One-hot encoding" is a way to represent categorical data (like Site A, Site B, Site C) in a mathematical model. By including site as a covariate, we statistically control for the fact that some participants were scanned at Site A and others at Site B, ensuring that any differences we find are due to ASD vs. TD, not the MRI machine.

the connectivity of the thalamus to bilateral pre- and post-central gyrus and the left superior parietal lobule is disrupted in ASD adolescents in response to aversive auditory and tactile stimuli $^{59}$ . Indeed, atypical thalamic connectivity to sensorimotor cortical regions is widely replicated in studies of children and adolescents with ASD $^{18,19,33,34,57}$ . Thus, our results demonstrate the presence of atypical thalamocortical connectivity to sensorimotor regions in HFASD and reinforce the notion that atypical thalamocortical connectivity is a neural correlate of sensorimotor processing differences in ASD.

To unpack this, let’s first clarify the key players. The **thalamus** acts as the brain’s central relay station, filtering and routing sensory information (like touch and sound) to the appropriate areas of the cortex. The **pre- and post-central gyri** are the primary motor and somatosensory cortices, respectively—essentially the brain’s control centers for movement and touch. The **superior parietal lobule** integrates sensory information to help us understand where our body is in space. When we say connectivity is "disrupted," we mean the communication lines between these hubs are not operating with the typical strength or pattern seen in neurotypical individuals. By linking this specific disruption to "aversive" (unpleasant) stimuli, we highlight that the issue isn't just about receiving a signal, but how the brain processes the emotional or sensory weight of that signal. This finding is crucial because it moves beyond simple anatomical differences to show a functional breakdown in how sensory experiences are processed, providing a strong neural explanation for the sensory sensitivities often reported by individuals with ASD.

While the link between sensory abnormalities and thalamocortical dysconnectivity seems to be clear, the effects of age on this relationship in ASD are unclear. Our post-hoc GLM analyses generally showed no significant main effect or interaction effect due to age. Hyperconnectivity between the thalami and sensorimotor regions was demonstrated in children and adolescents with ASD in several recent reports $^{18-20,33,57}$ , consistent with our finding in HFASD in this study. To fully understand the effects of age on thalamocortical dysconnectivity, we will need to perform further investigations using a longitudinal design.

Here, we encounter a critical methodological nuance. **Post-hoc GLM (General Linear Model) analyses** are statistical tests performed after the main experiment to check for additional variables, in this case, age. The fact that we found no significant effect of age suggests that the thalamocortical connectivity differences we observed are stable across the age range studied, rather than being a transient developmental phase. This is a significant finding because it implies that this neural signature is a persistent feature of ASD, not just a temporary fluctuation during childhood. However, the authors wisely note a limitation: cross-sectional studies (looking at different people at one point in time) cannot fully capture how these connections change *within* an individual as they grow. Therefore, **longitudinal designs**—tracking the same individuals over years—are necessary to map the trajectory of this dysconnectivity. This distinction is vital for understanding whether these neural patterns are fixed traits or dynamic processes that evolve with maturation.

In addition to age, sex is known to drive considerable variation in the clinical presentation of ASD $^{60}$ . Acknowledging our modest sample size, we explored potential sex differences in our observed brain-behavior relations and report preliminary observations (see Fig. 2B, C and Supplemental Information). We found that ASD males exhibited a positive correlation between sensorimotor thalamocortical connectivity and AQ, while ASD females exhibited a negative correlation. Furthermore, for males but not females, the thalamocortical connectivity partially mediated the ASD vs. TD group difference in AQ. This suggests that sensorimotor function may affect ASD characteristics differentially by sex in adults with ASD. In fact, a recent meta-analysis revealed that high-functioning female adults with ASD typically report disproportionately more sensorimotor symptoms than their ASD male counterparts $^{61}$ . A potential mechanism of sex differences in sensorimotor processing could be differences in inhibitory neurotransmission. In our previous study of GABA concentrations in HFASD, we observed that ASD males had a negative correlation of thalamic GABA concentration with AQ, but ASD females had a positive correlation, a similar sex-specific relationship as observed in the present study $^{24}$ . Altogether, these preliminary results, in conjunction with the findings from past studies, demonstrate the impact of sex on ASD neurobiology and underscore the need for investigating sex differences in studies of ASD.

This section introduces a profound and often overlooked variable: **sex**. The **AQ (Autism Quotient)** is a standardized measure of autistic traits. The finding here is counterintuitive and highly significant: the relationship between brain connectivity and autistic traits flips depending on sex. In males, higher connectivity correlated with higher AQ scores (more traits), whereas in females, higher connectivity correlated with lower AQ scores. This "mirror image" effect suggests that the same neural circuitry may function differently in males and females, or that different compensatory mechanisms are at play. The term **mediated** means that the connectivity acts as an intermediary; it explains *why* there is a difference in AQ scores between the ASD and TD (Typical Development) groups. The authors connect this to **GABA**, the brain's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, which acts like a brake on neural activity. The fact that GABA levels show a similar sex-specific correlation with AQ in previous studies strengthens the hypothesis that **inhibitory neurotransmission**—the brain's ability to dampen signals—is a key biological driver of these sex differences. This is a critical insight because it warns researchers that lumping males and females together in ASD studies can obscure these distinct biological pathways, leading to incomplete or misleading conclusions.

The presence of thalamocortical hyperconnectivity further suggests awry inhibitory mechanisms. Inhibitory neurons in the thalamus are known to counter the synchronizing tendency of excitatory thalamocortical neurons, mediated by GABA $_{A}$ receptors $^{62}$ . In fact, our earlier study on the same cohort using proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed decreased thalamic concentrations of GABA in ASD males compared to their TD counterparts $^{24}$ . Additionally, GABA has previously been associated with the integrity of synchronized oscillations in sensory processing $^{16}$ . While hyperconnectivity may indicate altered function in the GABAergic system in the thalamus, biophysical modeling is needed to explore the mechanisms of how thalamic inhibition can impact thalamocortical functional connectivity $^{63}$ .

Let’s dive deeper into the mechanics of **hyperconnectivity**. Normally, the thalamus uses a balance of excitatory (go) and inhibitory (stop) signals to filter noise and ensure that only relevant sensory information reaches the cortex. **GABA $_{A}$ receptors** are the specific molecular targets for GABA that facilitate this inhibition. If the inhibitory "brakes" are faulty or weakened (as suggested by the decreased GABA concentrations found in ASD males), the excitatory signals may become overly synchronized or "stuck" in a high-activity state. This results in **hyperconnectivity**—not necessarily because the wires are stronger, but because the filtering mechanism is failing, leading to excessive, unfiltered communication. This is analogous to a radio with a broken volume control; the signal isn't necessarily stronger at the source, but the receiver is amplifying it too much because the limiter is broken. The authors correctly note that while we can measure this connectivity and the GABA levels, we need **biophysical modeling** to simulate exactly how these molecular changes translate into the network-level connectivity patterns we observe. This highlights the gap between chemical measurements and functional outcomes.

Our results indicate group differences in functional connectivity of the right thalamus but not the left. Similar asymmetries have been found previously in a study of children with ASD, which observed greater white matter compromise, greater thalamic functional specialization, and maladaptive temporo-thalamic hyperconnectivity in the right hemisphere $^{57}$ . To rule out the possibility of a mediating effect of handedness, we ensured that the proportion of individuals with ASD who were right-handed did not differ significantly from that of controls (Table 1). Other explanations for this asymmetry may be found through other studies of the thalamus in ASD. One study investigating serotonin levels in thalamic pathways finds asymmetries in children with ASD in serotonin synthesis in the thalamus, frontal cortex, and dentate gyrus $^{64}$ . Interestingly, serotonin has been previously implicated in the hyperexcitability of sensory thalamocortical circuits $^{65}$ . Thus, the asymmetry of thalamic hyperconnectivity with the sensorimotor cortex further suggests an underlying disruption of neurotransmitter systems in the thalamus.

Why is the **right thalamus** specifically affected? The brain is lateralized, meaning the left and right hemispheres often specialize in different functions. The fact that the connectivity difference is isolated to the right side suggests a specific, localized disruption rather than a global one. The authors carefully control for **handedness**, a common confounding variable in brain studies, ensuring that the asymmetry isn't just a byproduct of motor dominance. They then pivot to another neurotransmitter: **serotonin**. Serotonin is involved in mood, sleep, and sensory processing. The discovery of asymmetric serotonin synthesis in the thalamus of children with ASD provides a potential chemical explanation for the right-sided hyperconnectivity. Since serotonin can influence the excitability of sensory circuits, its uneven distribution could be the root cause of the right-hemisphere-specific connectivity issues. This connects the dots between molecular chemistry (serotonin levels), structural asymmetry (right vs. left), and functional outcome (hyperconnectivity), painting a multi-layered picture of the neurobiology of ASD.

Future investigations ought to examine the connectivity of specific thalamic nuclei to further elucidate the relationship between thalamocortical connectivity and sensorimotor function in ASD. Fifth, the lack of measures for sensorimotor symptoms could limit the extension of our conclusions to impaired sensorimotor processing in ASD. In future studies, we will prioritize the characterization of sensorimotor symptoms accordingly. Lastly, the use of only self-report measures may be problematic due to the subjectivity of reporting symptom severity.
Despite these limitations, this study reports findings of resting-state thalamocortical functional hyperconnectivity with the sensorimotor regions in HFASD for the first time. This hyperconnectivity is associated with autistic features across all participants. These results confirm existing literature on the widespread hyperconnectivity of the thalamus with the cortex and strongly suggest the presence of differences in sensorimotor processing in ASD. These differences could be indicative of disrupted neurotransmitter systems in the thalamus and can be attributed to the neurobiology of ASD independent of typically associated cognitive differences and age. Further investigation into the underlying mechanisms of disrupted thalamocortical connectivity and how it may lead to sex-specific abnormal sensory processing is encouraged.
